full_judgment:
6. Mr AQ Md Shafiullah, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No.2, assisted by his junior Advocate Mr Mohammad Ullah, submits that while the petitioners was Branch Manager of the Cox's Bazar City Bank, he committed criminal breach of trust violating instructions of the bank by extending several loan amounts beyond his financial power for illegal gain. He submits that the Government has 49% share in the capital of the Bank and, as such, every officer of the City Bank is treated as public servant within meaning of section 21 of the Penal Code and section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. In this aspect, the learned Advocate has cited a case decision reported in 1999 BLD (AD) 234. On the question of civil liability in the transaction, it is submitted that money suit filed against the accused petitioner was for realization of money and not for offence and both civil and criminal cases can run together, and the relief  available in the civil Court does not stand as a bar to initiate a criminal proceedings if it is found by the disclosure of facts that there is distinct element of criminal offence in the matter. 

 9. Next question raised is that the petitioner was an officer of a private Bank and, as such, he was not a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Penal Code read with section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and, as such, the learned Special Judge has the jurisdiction to hold trial of the petitioner-accused under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958. In this respect, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the City Bank submits that the Government invested 49% of the total capital of the City Bank and the officer serving in the said Bank may accordingly be treated as a public servant in view of clause 12(b) of section 21 of the Penal Code as amended in 1982. The learned Advocate also cited case decision in support of his contention. It appears from the petition of complaint (Annexure-A) that the Government has share capital in the Bank and there is no challenge from the other side in this aspect. It is clear from section 21(12)(b) of the Penal Code as amended in the year 1982 that in any private firm or company in which the Government has interest or share capital, the employees of such organisation shall be considered as public servant. In the case of International Finance and Investment & Commerce Bank Limited vs Abdul Quayum and another reported in 1999 BLD (AD) 234 it has already been decided that the persons having service in those type of private financial institutions are to be treated as public servant under section 21 of the Penal Code and section 2 of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. There is no doubt about it that the petitioner- accused, while discharging function as public servant, had committed the alleged offence according to the prosecution case. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that when the City Bank Limited already instituted 2 money suits for recovery of loans from the two loanees and got decree vide the Annexure-D series, no further criminal proceeding in respect of the said money is maintainable. But such type of argument is not at all acceptable. The transaction of extending loan, no doubt, gives rise to civil liability as well; because there is no way out but to file money suit for the purpose of recovery of loan, but that does not create any bar to initiate criminal prosecution if the person is also liable to a criminal charge and necessary elements of such offence are found present. So, in certain cases one person may have to bear civil as well as criminal liability for the same occurrence. In the present case, the petitioner has been prosecuted for criminal offence with specific disclosure of allegations, which obviously attract criminal offence too. In support of this contention, a case decision reported in 48 DLR (AD) 100 may be referred to. 

 10. Though the learned Advocate for the petitioner has not taken any specific ground regarding legal requirement of sanction, he has raised the question at the time of making submission. It appears from the lower court records that the Senior Special Judge directly took cognisance in this case under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 by an order dated 9-11-94 and no prior sanction of the Government was taken before initiation of such proceeding against the public servant in accordance with section 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958. It is true that without prior sanction, the special judge has no legal authority to take cognisance and issue process against any public servant. But on perusal of the record, it appears that the leaned Special Judge took cognisance on 9-11- 94, while the petitioner was no more in the service of the City Bank. Admittedly, he was dismissed from Bank service on 24-7-91 and he was not a public servant at the time when cognisance was taken in this case. It has been settled law in our jurisdiction that if the accused has ceased to be a public servant at the time when the court took cognisance, no sanction of the Government is necessary to proceed against him. It is decided in the case of GM Towab, Air Vice-Marshal (Reid) vs State reported in 34 DLR 390 that since the accused was no longer in the service as public servant when the court took cognisance of the offence, sanction was not necessary. So, when the accused petitioner was no longer a public servant, the requirement of sanction as contemplated under 6(5) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958, has no manner of application.
